results.name: outside_range_yes_multi
results.description: Yes rate for targets outside [min, max] of the examples on sets with 3-4 examples; observed above null means the model is too confident that rich example sets exclude out-of-range numbers (under-generalizes beyond the range), below means it over-generalizes.
results.code:
# name: outside_range_yes_multi
# description: Yes rate for targets outside [min, max] of the examples on sets with 3-4 examples; observed above null means the model is too confident that rich example sets exclude out-of-range numbers (under-generalizes beyond the range), below means it over-generalizes.
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4))
    ex = ex.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: within_cell_response_variability
results.description: Mean over (set, target) cells of p(1-p), p = cell yes rate across repeated presentations; observed above null means the model's predicted probabilities are too extreme (near 0/1) relative to graded human responding, below means too graded.

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Yes rate in the second half of trial_index minus the first half (median split); observed differing from null (~0) means a session-time drift in yes-bias that the stationary model cannot produce (positive = humans say yes more later on).

results.name: recency_order_effect
results.description: For sets with 2+ examples and non-example targets, yes rate when the target is nearer the last-shown example than the first minus when nearer the first; observed differing from null (~0) means presentation order matters to humans (positive = recency) which the order-invariant model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: recency_order_effect
# description: For sets with 2+ examples and non-example targets, yes rate when the target is nearer the last-shown example than the first minus when nearer the first; observed differing from null (~0) means presentation order matters to humans (positive = recency) which the order-invariant model cannot produce.
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4))
    ex = ex.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1).astype(int)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(t)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    isin = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    df_, dl = np.abs(t - first), np.abs(t - last)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~isin
    a, b = base & (dl < df_), base & (df_ < dl)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: single_example_far_target_yes
results.description: Yes rate for single-example sets on targets more than 30 away from the example; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from one example to distant numbers, below means too broadly.

# name: single_example_far_target_yes
# description: Yes rate for single-example sets on targets more than 30 away from the example; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from one example to distant numbers, below means too broadly.
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4))
    ex = ex.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):

    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    m = (n == 1) & (np.abs(t - ex[:, 0]) > 30)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: distance_gradient_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes on distance (in tens) from target to nearest example, among targets not in the set; observed more negative than null means humans show a steeper numeric-similarity gradient than the model, more positive means a flatter (or reversed) one.
results.code:
# name: distance_gradient_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes on distance (in tens) from target to nearest example, among targets not in the set; observed more negative than null means humans show a steeper numeric-similarity gradient than the model, more positive means a flatter (or reversed) one.
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4))
    ex = ex.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = d > 0
    x, y = d[m] / 10.0, r[m]
    if m.sum() < 3 or x.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(x, y, bias=True)[0, 1] / x.var())
